To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the following factors are associated with an increased likelihood of a patient remaining abstinent from smoking at one year: a higher number of sessions of behavioural support; higher intensity of behavioural support; and use of nicotine replacement therapy.
• Smokers are most likely to stop if they receive a combination of behavioural support (including carbon monoxide monitoring) and medication.
the best way to stop smoking is: 'Stop smoking now and get advice from your GP'.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following questions: 1) What is the impact of a brief smoking cessation intervention on the health of smokers?
the development and evaluation of a range of interventions for smoking cessation.

the following questions: What is the role of the GP in helping patients to quit smoking? How effective is smoking cessation advice from GPs and what factors are associated with its effectiveness? What is the best way to deliver smoking cessation advice to patients? What are the most effective ways to deliver smoking cessation interventions to smokers? What are the best ways of delivering smoking cessation interventions in primary care settings? What are the barriers to the delivery of smoking cessation interventions by health professionals?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the GP is a key player in helping patients stop smoking.

GPs should: Offer advice on stopping smoking to all smokers, including those who have stopped within the past year; Use carbon monoxide monitoring to assess the smoker's progress and provide feedback to the patient; Provide advice on the most suitable smoking cessation medication; Help smokers to set a clear 'not-a-puff' rule.
GPs should offer all their patients advice on smoking cessation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the most effective way of delivering smoking cessation advice to smokers is by a combination of behavioural support and the use of smoking cessation medication.
smoking cessation is the single most cost effective intervention for the reduction in premature mortality.

we have shown the importance of behavioural support for smoking cessation, and that the behavioural support should be delivered by a healthcare professional with a good knowledge of smoking cessation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
GPs should be confident in their ability to help patients stop smoking and that they should not be afraid of using medication, even for the first attempt.
GPs can make a real difference to the health of their patients by helping them stop smoking, said Professor John Britton, director of the Tobacco Advisory Group.
GPs have a key role to play in helping patients to quit.
